title: Jeremiah 35:1–19
context: The narrator sets this episode in the days of Jehoiakim, earlier than chapter 34. The LORD tells Jeremiah to bring the Rechabites into a room in the LORD’s house and offer them wine (35:1–2). From 35:3, Jeremiah speaks in the first person, describing how he set bowls of wine before them, and the Rechabites reply that their father Jonadab son of Rechab commanded them to drink no wine, build no houses, sow no seed, plant no vineyard, and live in tents; they have obeyed, coming into Jerusalem only for fear of the invading armies (35:6–11). The narrator elsewhere mentions a Jehonadab son of Rechab in the days of Jehu (2 Kings 10:15, 10:23), and many identify him with this Jonadab, though Jeremiah 35 does not say so. The LORD then uses the Rechabites as an object lesson: they keep their father’s command, but Judah has not listened to the LORD, who has spoken to them repeatedly and sent his prophets (35:12–17). Jeremiah closes with a promise to the Rechabites that Jonadab will not lack a man to stand before the LORD forever (35:18–19). Both traditions read the chapter as shared ground about faithful obedience, without turning the Rechabites’ particular way of life into a rule for readers.

verses.text: The word which came to Jeremiah from the LORD in the days of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The word came “in the days of Jehoiakim.” Arminian readers note that this episode is earlier than chapter 34. The book arranges material by theme as well as by time, setting the Rechabites’ obedience beside Judah’s broken covenant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the earlier date and the thematic placement. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as introducing an object lesson in faithfulness, placed after the account of the broken slave-release covenant.

verses.text: “Go to the house of the Rechabites, and speak to them, and bring them into the LORD’s house, into one of the rooms, and give them wine to drink.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Jeremiah to bring the Rechabites into the LORD’s house and give them wine. Arminian readers note that the test is set up as a public sign. The LORD knows the Rechabites will refuse, and the refusal is the lesson.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the scene as a prophetic sign arranged by the LORD. Shared ground: both traditions read the command as an object lesson, not as a temptation to sin, and both see the temple setting as making the lesson public.

verses.text: Then I took Jaazaniah the son of Jeremiah, the son of Habazziniah, with his brothers, all his sons, and the whole house of the Rechabites;
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah takes Jaazaniah, his brothers, his sons, and the whole house of the Rechabites. Arminian readers note that Jeremiah now speaks in the first person. The whole family is included, showing a shared commitment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the inclusion of the whole household. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the narrative setup, and neither builds conclusions on the names beyond what the text gives.

verses.text: and I brought them into the LORD’s house, into the room of the sons of Hanan the son of Igdaliah, the man of God, which was by the room of the princes, which was above the room of Maaseiah the son of Shallum, the keeper of the threshold.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah brings them into the room of the sons of Hanan, by the room of the princes. Arminian readers note the careful detail of the setting. The test takes place in a known location within the temple, among witnesses.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the specific and public place. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as historical detail that roots the sign in a real place, and neither presses the details beyond the narrator’s description.

verses.text: I set before the sons of the house of the Rechabites bowls full of wine, and cups; and I said to them, “Drink wine!”
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah sets out bowls of wine and says, “Drink wine!” Arminian readers note the directness of the offer. The prophet presents the test plainly, so that the Rechabites’ answer will be clear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the test set in the open. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as staging the object lesson, and both note that wine itself is not condemned here; the lesson concerns the Rechabites’ faithfulness to their father’s command.

verses.text: But they said, “We will drink no wine; for Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, commanded us, saying, ‘You shall drink no wine, neither you nor your children, forever.
verses.arminianNotes: “We will drink no wine; for Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, commanded us.” Arminian readers note the Rechabites’ steady loyalty. They refuse even in the LORD’s house, at the prophet’s invitation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see faithfulness to an ancestral command. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing obedience held firmly, and neither treats abstaining from wine as a rule binding on readers.

verses.text: You shall not build a house, sow seed, plant a vineyard, or have any; but all your days you shall dwell in tents, that you may live many days in the land in which you live as nomads.’
verses.arminianNotes: Jonadab commanded them not to build houses, sow seed, or plant vineyards, but to live in tents. Arminian readers note the distinctive way of life. The text gives the command without explaining its reasons.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the reasons for Jonadab’s command are not stated. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing the Rechabites’ particular calling, without making it a pattern required of others.

verses.text: We have obeyed the voice of Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, in all that he commanded us, to drink no wine all our days, we, our wives, our sons, or our daughters;
verses.arminianNotes: “We have obeyed the voice of Jonadab… in all that he commanded us.” Arminian readers note the completeness of their obedience, including wives, sons, and daughters, across generations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a household united in obedience. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the heart of the object lesson: a family that keeps a human father’s command faithfully.

verses.text: and not to build houses for ourselves to dwell in. We have no vineyard, field, or seed;
verses.arminianNotes: They have no houses, vineyard, field, or seed. Arminian readers note the costly nature of their obedience. Their way of life sets them apart from their neighbors and requires sacrifice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the cost of faithfulness. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the Rechabites’ testimony, and both see in it an example of steady commitment rather than a lifestyle to copy.

verses.text: but we have lived in tents, and have obeyed, and done according to all that Jonadab our father commanded us.
verses.arminianNotes: They say, “we have lived in tents, and have obeyed.” Arminian readers note the simple summary of their faithfulness. Their obedience is not occasional but a settled pattern of life over many years.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a life shaped by obedience. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as completing the Rechabites’ account of their faithfulness, which the LORD will contrast with Judah’s refusal to listen.

verses.text: But when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up into the land, we said, ‘Come! Let’s go to Jerusalem for fear of the army of the Chaldeans, and for fear of the army of the Syrians; so we will dwell at Jerusalem.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: They came to Jerusalem “for fear of the army of the Chaldeans.” Arminian readers note the practical exception. Their presence in the city was a response to danger, not a rejection of their father’s command.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a reasonable response to invasion. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as explaining why the Rechabites were in Jerusalem, and neither treats it as a breach of their obedience.

verses.text: Then the LORD’s word came to Jeremiah, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: “Then the LORD’s word came to Jeremiah.” Arminian readers note the turn from the scene to its meaning. The LORD now interprets the sign for Judah and Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD explaining the object lesson. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as introducing the application of the sign, which concerns Judah’s failure to listen.

verses.text: “The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says: ‘Go and tell the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, “Will you not receive instruction to listen to my words?” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “Will you not receive instruction to listen to my words?” Arminian readers note the LORD’s pleading question. He invites Judah to learn from what they have seen.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the LORD’s call to receive instruction. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a real appeal to Judah, using the Rechabites’ example to expose the people’s refusal to listen.

verses.text: “The words of Jonadab the son of Rechab that he commanded his sons, not to drink wine, are performed; and to this day they drink none, for they obey their father’s commandment; but I have spoken to you, rising up early and speaking, and you have not listened to me.
verses.arminianNotes: The Rechabites obey their father’s command, “but I have spoken to you… and you have not listened to me.” Arminian readers note the sharp contrast. A human father is obeyed, but the LORD is not.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the contrast between faithful children and an unfaithful people. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the center of the lesson and apply it as a call to listen to God.

verses.text: I have sent also to you all my servants the prophets, rising up early and sending them, saying, ‘Every one of you must return now from his evil way, amend your doings, and don’t go after other gods to serve them. Then you will dwell in the land which I have given to you and to your fathers;’ but you have not inclined your ear, nor listened to me.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD sent his prophets, saying, “Every one of you must return now from his evil way.” Arminian readers note the repeated call to repentance with a promise of dwelling in the land. The people were given real opportunity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s patient and repeated warnings. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing God’s persistent call to return, and both see the people’s refusal to incline their ear as culpable.

verses.text: The sons of Jonadab the son of Rechab have performed the commandment of their father which he commanded them, but this people has not listened to me.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: The Rechabites performed their father’s command, “but this people has not listened to me.” Arminian readers note the repetition that drives home the contrast. Faithfulness is possible, as the Rechabites show.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the repeated contrast as emphasizing Judah’s guilt. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as summarizing the object lesson, without turning it into a rule for readers beyond the call to obey God.

verses.text: “Therefore the LORD, the God of Armies, the God of Israel, says: ‘Behold, I will bring on Judah and on all the inhabitants of Jerusalem all the evil that I have pronounced against them, because I have spoken to them, but they have not heard; and I have called to them, but they have not answered.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: “I will bring on Judah… all the evil that I have pronounced against them.” Arminian readers note that judgment follows refusal: “I have called to them, but they have not answered.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see judgment as a just response to persistent refusal. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly as the consequence of not listening, and both see the LORD’s many calls as part of his patience.

verses.text: Jeremiah said to the house of the Rechabites, “The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says: ‘Because you have obeyed the commandment of Jonadab your father, and kept all his precepts, and done according to all that he commanded you,’
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah speaks to the Rechabites, commending them for obeying Jonadab. Arminian readers note that faithfulness is honored. The LORD sees and values the Rechabites’ steady obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s commendation of their faithfulness. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that obedience is noticed and honored by God, and both see the Rechabites as an example rather than a rule.

verses.text: therefore the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says: ‘Jonadab the son of Rechab will not lack a man to stand before me forever.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: “Jonadab the son of Rechab will not lack a man to stand before me forever.” Arminian readers note the promise of an enduring line that serves before the LORD, a blessing on faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a gracious promise to a faithful family. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a word of blessing, and neither speculates about later Rechabites beyond what the text states.
